common_name: Will Fleming Yaupon Holly (Narrow Columnar Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, upright male selection of native yaupon holly that never needs shearing to maintain its columnar shape.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, strictly upright, columnar selection of the Gulf Coast native yaupon holly, discovered and named for a Texas landscape architect, and valued for providing the vertical accent of a formal columnar evergreen without any shearing or shaping required to maintain the shape. As a male selection it does not produce the red berries typical of yaupon holly, but its extreme drought tolerance, adaptability to both wet and dry soils, and complete indifference to heat and poor soil make it one of the toughest, most maintenance-free narrow accent shrubs available for Gulf Coast gardens. It works well as a narrow screen, foundation accent, or repeated vertical element along a walk or drive.

common_name: Schillings Dwarf Yaupon Holly (Compact Rounded Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Schillings Dwarf is a naturally compact, dense, mounding male selection of native yaupon holly that needs little to no shearing to stay tidy.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Schillings Dwarf (also sold as Stokes Dwarf) is one of the most widely planted compact hollies in the Gulf South, a naturally dense, rounded, slow-growing selection of native yaupon that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mass plantings without the constant shearing that fast-growing shrubs demand. Being a male selection it does not set the red berries of the species, but it more than compensates with an extremely low-maintenance, uniformly rounded habit and outstanding tolerance of heat, drought, wind, salt spray, and poor soil, making it a workhorse plant across coastal Gulf landscapes. Established plants need very little supplemental water and only occasional light shearing if a stricter formal shape is desired.

common_name: Soft Touch Holly (Spineless Dwarf Mounding Japanese Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Soft Touch has soft, spineless foliage unlike most hollies and a naturally low, rounded mounding habit that needs minimal pruning.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Soft Touch is a Japanese holly selection valued for its genuinely soft, spineless foliage, pleasant to brush against or work around unlike the prickly leaves of Chinese hollies, combined with a naturally dense, low, rounded mounding habit that stays tidy with little to no pruning. Its fine-textured, boxwood-like appearance makes it a popular low-maintenance substitute for boxwood in foundation plantings and low borders, especially in humid climates where boxwood can struggle with disease. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil and tolerates a range of light conditions from partial shade to nearly full sun, needing only an occasional light shearing if a more formal outline is wanted.

common_name: Sky Pencil Holly (Extremely Narrow Columnar Japanese Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Sky Pencil grows in an extremely narrow, upright column, making it useful for tight spaces where a wide shrub will not fit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Sky Pencil is a striking Japanese holly selection with an extremely narrow, strictly upright, columnar growth habit unlike almost any other common shrub, reaching several feet tall while staying only a foot or so wide, which makes it a favorite for narrow side yards, tight entryway plantings, and repeated vertical accents flanking a doorway or path. The small, glossy, spineless leaves give it a refined, fine texture, and while it holds its narrow shape naturally, an occasional light shearing keeps individual plants uniform in a formal planting. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained soil, since it can struggle in soggy or very dry sites, and light staking when young helps prevent splaying in heavy snow or wind until the plant matures.
